messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I’ve gone too far down the rabbit hole and need some help. If you’re looking for a procrastination device, I’ve attached an .html file that has all the actual code involved so far, but really my question can be generalized at this point:

I’m trying to calculate transit times for my fish, and this operation seems to require for-loops because of the specific indexing of the rows involved (transit_time = arrival[i+1] - departure[i], for example).  I can do this successfully for a single fish track from a list of dataframes (one dataframe for each fish), but what is the best practice for applying for-loops to a list of dataframes?

For example, is it best to write the for-loop into a function, and then apply that function to the list of dataframes with lapply()?  Or is there some crazy list indexing I haven't learned that is common practice for this?  I started to write:

# d3 is the full fishtracks dataframe

d3split <- d3 %>%
   split(as.factor(.$TagID)) %>%
   map(cbind, transittime = "NA") # we now have a dataframe for each fish that has a column, "transittime" in each.

# for-loop to calculate transit_time:

for(i in 1:length(d3split)) {
   for(j in 1:length(d3split[[i]]$transittime)) {
           d3split[[i]]$transittime[j] = difftime(d3split[[i]]$arrival[j+1], d3split[[i]]$departure[j], units = "hours")
   }
}

… and realized I was probably either working too hard or not going to get the indexing right without help. Any thoughts?

PS - I know for-loops are rarely the answer, but if you're going to tell me not to use a for-loop, please give me a data-organization alternative as well. :)

Thanks so much!

Myfanwy
​
--

messages.body_plain:
I think you can lose the loops without messing with an internal j loop, as you can just shift one of the vectors in your difftime() function:
for(i in 1:length(d3split)) {
  d3split[[i]]$transittime <- difftime(c(d3split[[i]]$arrival[-1], NA), d3split[[i]]$departure, units="hours")
}

But this is eased by the lag() function, and dplyr has convenient alternate lead() and lag() functions that deal with the NA you get at the start and end of the vectors. So ultimately you don’t need to deal with this as a list at all:
d3 %>%
  group_by(TagID) %>%
  mutate(transittime = difftime(lead(arrival), departure, units="hours"))
​

messages.subject_clean: spatial analysis question -- IBD but not for genetic data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm searching for a spatial analysis that can compare a continuous variable (in my case, contaminant concentrations from sampled bird tissues) among sites and give some measure of relatedness of the concentrations based on distance between the sites. The primary question I want to answer is, "Are the observed concentrations at each site related to the distance between sites?" I believe it would be somewhat analogous to Isolation by Distance for you geneticists out there. I've checked out the Adegenet package in R, but am having a hard time exchanging the genetic data for my contaminant data. Also, I don't have an "expected" baseline of concentrations.

I'd love to hear any and all ideas for approaching this question in R. Appreciate your help!

Corey

messages.body_plain:
Is it distance between sites that really matters, or are you trying to determine if the concentration of a contaminant is spatially autocorrelated (i.e., there are some geographic areas that tend to have lots of contaminants, and others not so much)? You can calculate Moran's I (available out of the box in the `ape` package), which is an index of spatial autocorrelation that takes a distance matrix (either geographic or environmental distance can be used) and a numeric vector. More info here <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ape/vignettes/MoranI.pdf>.

Cheers,
Tad

messages.body_plain:
You’re right. Moran’s I will tell you if there is global autocorrelation in your dataset. However, even if there is no global autocorrelation, sites close to one another may have similar values. You may want to investigate local spatial autocorrelation measures. There are local Moran’s I, Getis-Ord local statistic. There are variants of these too. See the following for pointers: https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/Spatial.html

Jon

Hey D-Ruggites!

I'll be giving a short presentation tomorrow about unit testing (and really testing in general).  This is an incredibly important aspect of coding that often gets skipped over by us non-software development types.  My goal is for you to walk away with a good understanding of the thinking process behind good testing.  I also hope to convince you that testing is not only in your best interest, but is also waaaay easier to integrate with your existing workflow than you might think.

The talk will be from ~1:00-1:30pm in Wickson 2124, and we'll have our regular work session after that.  Bring your questions and R problems!

I'll send the webcast link and github repo link tomorrow!  For now:

credit: Randall Munroe

Hi Mike,

my 2c -- I don't know Flask that well, but I've worked extensively with
previous Python web stacks.

Flask and D3 *can* do pretty much anything, it's true!  It's a pretty
standard web stack in the Python world and it's incredibly flexible
(i.e. permits all the things).

The downside is that you can do pretty much anything -- which means there's
a lot more up-front complexity and the learning curve is both steeper and
potentially a lot deeper.

Personally I'd shy away from something so general unless I could identify a few
specific things that I know I want to do that are difficult or impossible in
Shiny.  But on the flip side learning Flask and d3 would open up a lot of
career options :)

Oh, and JavaScript (used for d3) is insane.  You'd be learning two new
languages!

cheers,
--titus

messages.body_plain:
One of the big issues with Shiny is that you need an R session running somewhere to handle the calculations, and depending on where you host this, it can be a pain. When our lab looked into building a web app, Shiny was a pain compared to something built from Javascript. The primary reason was that the security issues behind having a web-facing R app was more than our IT department wanted to deal with. RStudio has their ShinyPro service that takes care of some of that, but you pay for it.

I think if it is something you want to distribute for people to run locally (on their machine, not yours), Shiny is a nice solution. As far as its limits, Duncan has some experience hacking Shiny to do new things not included in the default toolbox.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
HI There,
I am don't have really any experience with coding other than in R, so I can't speak to the other methods/languages you have been discussing, but I did develop a custom Shiny app for a researcher on campus over the summer and fall. I was starting from scratch as I had never used Shiny or developed any sort of web app before. They needed a tool to help them analyze raw ICPMS data. The app allows the user to upload a raw ICPMS run file, does a bunch of analysis automatically to calculate the isotope ratios, and then allows the user change several parameters including subsetting the data interactively by highlighting it in on a plot displayed in the app, downloads the plot to the users machine, and uploads the subsetted summary data to the users google drive in a google sheet. I don't think this was very high level, but I do feel I was able to do whatever I wanted or needed Shiny to do, I just had to figure out how.

As for learning Shiny on my own, there are tons of video tutorials and Stack Overflow posts. If you know R well, I think Shiny is very user friendly.

Have you heard of shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>? You can host your app on R Studio servers and your app publishes easily to shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> from within R Studio once you have an account. Then you can send the link to the published app to anyone. They have a free version that allows 25 hours of app run time per month and 5 published apps. The next level up was only $9/month I think.The only trouble we have run into so far is that without the Pro version of shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> ($300/month), you can't define a custom URL, which is needed to have a google login button on your app.

Katie

*From:* csis-r...@ucdavis.edu <csis-r...@ucdavis.edu> on behalf of Mario Biagioli <mbia...@ucdavis.edu>
*Sent:* Monday, November 28, 2016 4:04 PM
*To:* cs...@ucdavis.edu
*Subject:* [CSIS] Ron Rivest talk, Thur 3pm, AUDITABILITY AND VERIFICATION OF ELECTIONS

On Thursday Prof. Ronald Rivest will give a talk “Auditability and Verification of Elections”.
Ron is one of the top computer scientists in the world. He has also been much in the news, in recent days, following the editorial he did with Philip Stark https://goo.gl/joF0lJ  .  Seating is limited.

*** CS Distinguished Lecturer  ***

Speaker:  Ronald L. Rivest, MIT
Title:    Auditability and Verification of Elections
Date:     Thursday, December 1, 2016
Time:     3:10 pm (reception starts at 2:30 pm)
Where:    1131 Kemper Hall
Host:     Phil Rogaway
Poster:   https://goo.gl/jeM6eu

Abstract: Democracy requires that elections have credible results—otherwise the winner lacks a political mandate and the supporters of losing candidates react with anything from protests to revolution.

Yet (U.S.) elections have become larger and increasingly complex, and politics seems more polarized. Software-based voting systems inspire little trust. Voting systems purchased with funds allocated after the 2000 U.S. presidential election fiasco are rapidly becoming obsolete.

How can good definitions, statistics, and cryptography help?

We present the notion of software independence, describe several methods for effective auditing of paper ballots, and give an overview of “end-to-end” cryptographic voting systems that allow voters to confirm that their votes were counted exactly as intended, without violating voter privacy or enabling vote-selling. We close with a (pessimistic) assessment of the prospects for “voting over the internet”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bio: Professor Rivest is an Institute Professor at MIT, a member of its Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), a member of that lab’s Theory of Computation Group and a leader of its Cryptography and Information Security Group.

He received a B.A. in Mathematics from Yale University in 1969, and a Ph.D. in Computer Science from Stanford University in 1974.

Rivest is a co-inventor of the RSA public-key cryptosystem, has extensive experience in cryptographic design and cryptanalysis. He is also a founder of RSA Data Security and of Verisign. Together with Adi Shamir and Len Adleman, he has received the 2002 ACM Turing Award.

He is also well-known as a co-author of the text, “Introduction to Algorithms” (with Cormen, Leiseron, and Stein).

He is a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the National Academy of Sciences, and is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery, the International Association for Cryptographic Research, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
He is on the Advisory Board for the Electronic Privacy Information Center and on the board of Verified Voting.

His research interests include cryptography, computer and network security, algorithms, and voting system security. His recent research emphasizes election integrity—methods involving statistical audits and methods based on the “end-to-end verifiable voting” paradigm.
--

Myfanwy Johnston
Ph.D Candidate, UC Davis
Animal Behavior Graduate Group
Biotelemetry Laboratory
